HuYgTa-190886-d1e114.summary: Title line of the question for Distinctions 24-25: whether falsehood can underlie faith.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e123.summary: Fragmentary printed marginal heading ('Resolutio'), apparently a misplaced or truncated label for the summary resolution that appears later; it carries no content of its own.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e132.summary: Formal statement of the question: whether falsehood can underlie faith, i.e. whether something false can fall under the assent of faith.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e138.summary: Opening argument for the affirmative: falsehood can underlie hope, so it can also underlie faith, since both are theological virtues. The antecedent is proved by the case of a foreknown (reprobate) person who hopes to be saved, whose hope is false because God's foreknowledge is infallible.
claims: If falsehood can underlie hope, it can underlie faith, since both are theological virtues.
The hope of a reprobate to be saved is false, given God's infallible foreknowledge.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e151.summary: Argument sed contra and plan of the question. No falsehood can underlie humanly acquired science (Posterior Analytics), and divinely infused faith is more infallible than acquired science, so no falsehood can underlie it. The author then divides the question into four articles: the object of faith; the question itself (for d. 24); the number and identity of the articles of faith; and the faith required under the law of nature and the Mosaic law (for d. 25, misprinted as 35).
claims: Falsehood cannot underlie acquired scientia, so a fortiori it cannot underlie divinely infused faith.
Infused faith is more infallible than humanly acquired science.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e175.summary: Printed summary resolution of the whole question: Catholic infused faith, whose proper and principal object is God, the author of all truth, contains no falsehood whatever.
claims: Infused Catholic faith contains no falsehood.
God, the author of all truth, is the principal object of faith.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e188.summary: Opens Article 1 on the object of faith by drawing a distinction from the object of science. 'Object' can mean what something is principally considered or known about, the incomplex subject of a demonstrated conclusion, or the complex thing known, i.e. the conclusion itself (whether principal or accessory). The same distinction applies to faith. The first conclusion is that, taking object in the first sense, God alone is the object of faith.
claims: The object of a science can be the incomplex subject of a conclusion or the complex conclusion itself.
In the first, proper sense, the object of faith is God alone.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e223.summary: First proof of the first conclusion: the principal object of Catholic faith is that about which we principally believe whatever is to be believed and to which all objects of belief are reduced, and God is such.
claims: All things to be believed are reduced to God as to that about which they are principally believed.
concepts: reduction of the credibilia to God

HuYgTa-190886-d1e236.summary: Second proof (continued in the next paragraph): the principal object of a theological virtue is uncreated being, which is what distinguishes theological virtues from naturally acquired virtues, whose principal object can be a created being. Faith is a theological virtue.
claims: The principal object of a theological virtue is uncreated being.
Theological virtues differ from acquired virtues by having uncreated being as their principal object.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e248.summary: Completes the second proof (faith is a theological virtue) and gives the third: the object of faith in this life is the same as that of clear vision in heaven, and the principal object of clear vision is God, so God alone is the principal object of faith.
claims: The object of faith in via is the same as the object of clear vision in patria.
God is the principal object of the beatific vision and so of faith.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e264.summary: Fourth proof from authority: Dionysius (De divinis nominibus 7) says divine faith concerns simple and ever-existing truth, which is God himself.
claims: Divine faith concerns simple, ever-existing truth, which is God.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e273.summary: First objection to the first conclusion: the Apostle defines faith as 'the substance of things hoped for', and what we hope for is our beatitude, which is something created, so faith seems to have a created object.
claims: Beatitude, the thing hoped for, appears to be something created.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e295.summary: Second objection: Augustine says faith concerns good and evil things, present, past and future, which seems to make created things its object.
claims: Faith seems, per Augustine, to extend to good and bad things of every time.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e302.summary: Replies to both objections. Beatitude can be taken formally, as a single created state, or objectively, as what makes us blessed: one in essence and three in persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit (per Augustine). In the second sense faith is called the substance of 'things' hoped for, so the plural refers to the divine persons. Augustine's remark about good and evil things does not concern the principal and formal object of faith.
claims: Beatitude taken objectively is the triune God, one in essence and three in persons.
The plural 'things hoped for' refers to the three divine persons.
Augustine's broad statement does not concern faith's principal and formal object.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e326.summary: Second conclusion of Article 1: taking object in the second, broad sense, as what is believed, all the articles of faith and much else annexed to them can be called objects of faith, since all must be believed for salvation, implicitly or explicitly.
claims: In the broad sense all the articles of faith and their annexes are objects of faith.
Such objects must be believed for salvation either implicitly or explicitly.

HuYgTa-190886-Dd1e181.summary: Article 1, on the object of faith. Distinguishing two senses of 'object', as for science, it concludes, first, that in the proper sense (that about which something is principally believed) God alone is the object of faith. This is proved by the reduction of all objects of belief to God, by the uncreated object proper to theological virtues, by the identity of the object of faith and of beatific vision, and by Dionysius. Objections from the Apostle's 'things hoped for' and Augustine's broad formula are answered by taking beatitude objectively as the triune God. Second, in the broad sense of what is believed, all the articles and their annexes are objects of faith, to be believed implicitly or explicitly.
claims: Properly speaking, God alone is the object of faith.
In the broad sense, the articles of faith and what is annexed to them are objects of faith.
Beatitude taken objectively is the triune God.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e349.summary: Rubric for Article 2: whether falsehood can underlie faith.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e358.summary: First conclusion of Article 2: no falsehood can underlie faith infused by God.
claims: No falsehood can underlie divinely infused faith.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e365.summary: First proof: God, the author of all created truth and uncreated truth itself, does not infuse into souls anything by which they could deviate from him; otherwise truth would mislead the one it instructs, a contradiction in terms.
claims: Uncreated truth cannot infuse a habit that leads away from truth.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e381.summary: Second proof from the modal status of faith's contents: a habit that posits only what is simply necessary, or what is contingent but considered as reduced to divine ordination, cannot be subject to falsehood. Contingents may fail to occur in themselves, but as ordained by God they occur necessarily. Faith posits only necessary truths about God ad intra, and contingent truths about God ad extra only as foreseen and ordained by God.
claims: Contingents considered as falling under divine ordination occur necessarily.
Faith posits necessary truths about God ad intra and contingent truths ad extra only as divinely foreseen and ordained.
Therefore no falsehood can underlie faith.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e414.summary: Third proof from the medium of assent: when someone assents to a conclusion through a medium that cannot fail, the assent cannot be false. The believer assents to the articles through the truth of divine authority, which cannot fail.
claims: Assent through an infallible medium cannot be false.
The believer assents to the articles through infallible divine authority.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e432.summary: Rejects a qualifying opinion that falsehood cannot underlie formed faith but can underlie unformed faith even when infused. Since its proponents offer no proof, the author denies it as easily as they assert it: any unformed faith by which someone believes falsehoods is not infused by God but feigned by the believer or acquired in some other way.
claims: Infused unformed faith is no more subject to falsehood than formed faith.
A faith by which someone believes falsehoods is not infused but feigned or acquired.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e455.summary: Introduces a series of objections raised by some directly against the first conclusion, without any distinction.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e462.summary: First objection: falsehood can underlie the prophetic light, which is clearer than a simple believer's faith, so it can underlie faith. Isaiah told Hezekiah he would die, yet the king lived fifteen more years, and Jonah announced that Nineveh would be overthrown in forty days, yet it was not.
claims: Prophecy, a higher light than faith, appears to have stated falsehoods.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e484.summary: Second objection: a believer living at the time of the Incarnation who, not knowing its moment, still believed Christ was yet to be incarnated, believed with the same faith something false.
claims: A believer ignorant of the moment of the Incarnation believed something false by the same faith.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e500.summary: Third objection: falsehood can underlie the act of latria that faith commands, as when a believer adores an unconsecrated host believing it consecrated; therefore it can underlie faith itself.
claims: Adoring an unconsecrated host seems to show that the act of latria commanded by faith can be false.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e511.summary: Fourth objection: after Abraham had faith in the liberation of the human race through Christ's passion, God could still have freed humanity in another way, so falsehood could have underlain Abraham's faith.
claims: God's ability to redeem otherwise seems to make Abraham's faith fallible.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e522.summary: Fifth objection from analogy with charity: an apparent but non-existent truth is no more repugnant to faith than an apparent but non-existent good is to charity, and charity can love a hypocrite who seems good but is evil. The author remarks that though heretics may argue against faith with such sophisms, all are easily answered once the foregoing is understood.
claims: By analogy with charity's love of a seeming good, faith might believe a seeming truth that is false.
Such arguments are sophisms easily answered by the foregoing.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e545.summary: Reply to the first objection: the prophets did not speak falsely. Isaiah spoke of Hezekiah's death according to the course of nature, seeing in prophetic light that neither art nor nature could save him; the later announcement of fifteen more years concerned divine power, not natural influence, so both statements were true. Jonah's prophecy was conditional, with the condition implied that Nineveh would fall if it did not repent; when the condition changed through penance, the city was spared without detriment to the prophecy's truth.
claims: Isaiah's prophecy of death concerned the course of nature, his later prophecy of life divine power.
Jonah's prophecy was conditional and remained true when Nineveh repented.
concepts: course of nature vs. divine power

HuYgTa-190886-d1e589.summary: Reply to the second objection: the belief that Christ was still to be incarnated after he was incarnated was elicited not by infused faith but by the believer's own opinion. Belief in a liberator was an act of faith in both testaments, but believing the precise hour of the Incarnation was not an act of faith under the Old Testament and was not required without special revelation. Under the New Testament we are bound to believe that he has come, because of the Scriptures and the Church's authority approving them.
claims: The erroneous belief came from opinion, not from infused faith.
Determinate belief about the time of the Incarnation was not required of Old Testament believers without revelation.
In the New Testament, belief that Christ has come rests on Scripture and the Church's authority.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e622.summary: Reply to the third objection: the act of latria is not simply adoration of the visible host, but adoration with a condition attached, actually or habitually: if the consecration was properly performed. Since faith commands the act with this condition, no falsehood ever underlies the act of latria as commanded by faith.
claims: Eucharistic adoration includes an implicit condition that the consecration was valid.
As commanded by faith, the act of latria is never false.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e640.summary: Reply to the fourth objection: although by his absolute power God could have freed humanity otherwise, the mode of redemption as reduced to divine ordination was simply unchangeable. Abraham's faith concerned the mode of liberation as it falls under God's ordained power, not his absolute power, so no falsehood underlay it.
claims: God could have redeemed otherwise by absolute power.
Under divine ordination the mode of redemption was immutable.
Faith concerns what falls under God's ordained power.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e662.summary: Reply to the fifth objection, denying both premises. Against the major: in loving by charity we rely on human cognition, which can be deceived, but in believing by faith we rely on divine authority, which is infallible. Against the minor: by infused charity we love a person not as he is in himself but as he is in God, and as existing in God everything is good, so even a feigned person is not loved as something feigned.
claims: Charity relies on fallible human cognition, faith on infallible divine authority.
Infused charity loves a person as he is in God, where everything is good.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e697.summary: Second conclusion of Article 2: falsehood can underlie acquired faith. This needs no separate proof beyond the opposites of the three reasons given for the first conclusion.
claims: Falsehood can underlie acquired faith.
Acquired faith lacks the conditions that make infused faith infallible.

HuYgTa-190886-Dd1e346.summary: Article 2 answers the question directly. First conclusion: no falsehood can underlie faith infused by God, since uncreated truth cannot infuse a deceiving habit, since faith posits only necessary truths or contingent truths as falling under divine ordination, and since it assents through infallible divine authority. The opinion that infused unformed faith can be false is rejected: such faith is feigned or acquired. Five objections are answered, from prophecy (Isaiah and Jonah spoke according to the course of nature or conditionally), from ignorance of the time of the Incarnation (a matter of opinion, not faith), from adoring an unconsecrated host (latria is implicitly conditional), from Abraham's faith (it concerned God's ordained, not absolute, power), and from charity's love of hypocrites (charity relies on human cognition and loves persons as they are in God). Second conclusion: falsehood can underlie acquired faith.
claims: No falsehood can underlie divinely infused faith, formed or unformed.
Contingent articles are infallible because they are believed as falling under divine ordination.
Faith concerns God's ordained, not his absolute, power.
Falsehood can underlie acquired faith.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e711.summary: Rubric for Article 3: how many and which are the articles of faith.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e720.summary: Explains the three creeds read in the Church. The Apostles' Creed was composed directly by the apostles, and its name 'symbolum' is etymologized as each apostle contributing his own portion (bolus) to a gathering. The Nicene Creed was composed at the Council of Nicaea, and the Athanasian Creed by Athanasius. The paragraph explains their liturgical use: the Apostles' Creed is said at Prime and Compline, signifying that a Christian must profess it from the beginning to the end of spiritual life, and is said silently because its truth was not yet openly preached in the early Church; it is called 'greater' for the dignity of its authors. The Nicene Creed is sung on feast days because faith was then solemnly revealed throughout the world, and the Athanasian Creed is said at morning, signifying that it was composed against the darkness of heretics.
claims: There are three creeds: the Apostles', the Nicene and the Athanasian.
The Apostles' Creed is greater by the dignity of its authors, not by the number of its words.
Each creed's liturgical use symbolizes its origin and purpose.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e775.summary: Although the same truth is expressed in all three creeds, more explicitly in the later two because of heretical cunning, the articles are customarily presented to the faithful as contained in the Apostles' Creed. Counted by their authors, there are twelve articles, one for each apostle, and the paragraph lists them with their traditional attributions: Peter (God the Father almighty, creator) through Matthias (resurrection of the flesh and eternal life).
claims: The three creeds express the same truth, the later ones more explicitly because of heresy.
Counted by their apostolic authors, there are twelve articles of faith.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e832.summary: Discusses an alternative enumeration. Counting by subject matter, some doctors give fourteen articles: seven on the divine nature, persons and works, and seven on Christ's humanity. Because this scheme makes God's unity and God as creator separate articles, though both are demonstrable, the author prefers the twelvefold apostolic division. He supports this with the Apostle (faith is of things not apparent), Augustine (faith is believing what you do not see) and Gregory (faith has no merit where human reason provides proof).
claims: Some doctors count fourteen articles, seven on divinity and seven on Christ's humanity.
God's unity and creatorship are demonstrable and therefore should not count as articles of faith.
The twelvefold division is preferable because faith concerns what is not demonstrated or seen.

HuYgTa-190886-Dd1e714.summary: Article 3, on the number of the articles of faith. It describes the three creeds (Apostles', Nicene, Athanasian), their origins, etymology and liturgical uses, and holds that they express the same truth with increasing explicitness against heresy. Counting by apostolic authors, there are twelve articles, attributed one to each apostle. The author rejects a fourteenfold division by subject matter because it counts demonstrable truths (God's unity and creatorship) as articles, which conflicts with faith's being of the unseen and undemonstrated.
claims: The articles of faith are best counted as twelve, following the Apostles' Creed.
Demonstrable truths such as God's unity are not properly articles of faith.
The three creeds express one faith with increasing explicitness.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e878.summary: Rubric for Article 4: the faith required under the law of nature and under the Mosaic law.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e891.summary: Answers Article 4 following Hugh of St Victor. Before the Mosaic law it was necessary for salvation to believe that God is creator and to expect salvation and redemption from him, though how it would come was unknown except to a few. Under the law a mediator was preached, but it was not yet clear whether he would be man, angel or God. Under grace the mode of redemption and the nature of the redeemer are openly preached. So before the Gospel explicit, distinct faith in each article was not necessary, since this was impossible without special revelation. There was, however, a measure of explicit belief within reach of natural reason enlightened by grace, which never fails an adult who places no obstacle and does what is in him: one God, creator, lord and ruler, not the author of evil, merciful to those who seek him, and a future redeemer. In short, after sin, a creator and a savior were to be believed, as Hebrews 11:6 suggests.
claims: Before the Gospel, explicit and distinct faith in every article was not necessary for salvation.
There was always a minimum of explicit belief: God as creator and as rewarding redeemer.
Grace sufficient for this measure was never lacking to an adult who did what was in him and placed no obstacle.
concepts: state of the law of nature

HuYgTa-190886-d1e981.summary: Two objections to the preceding answer. First, Augustine says the same faith in the Mediator that saves us also saved the ancients. Second, as charity relates to what is to be loved so faith relates to what is to be believed; the ancients needed charity toward everything we must love, so they needed faith in everything we must believe.
claims: Augustine teaches the identity of the faith of the ancients and of Christians.
The parallel with charity suggests the ancients needed explicit faith in everything we believe.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e1003.summary: Reply to the first objection: the faith of the ancients and of the moderns is the same, but it was not equally explicit or distinctly declared.
claims: The faith of the ancients and moderns is one, differing only in degree of explicitness.

HuYgTa-190886-d1e1012.summary: Reply to the second objection: the analogy fails, because natural instinct suffices for knowing what is to be loved, but not for knowing what is to be believed.
claims: Natural instinct suffices for the knowledge of what is to be loved but not of what is to be believed.
concepts: things to be loved vs. things to be believed

HuYgTa-190886-d1e1023.summary: Reply to the opening argument: its antecedent is false for true, infused hope. By such hope a person hopes for beatitude only presupposing merits, and whoever has merits at the end of life will be saved. So although a reprobate is not saved, the conditional 'if the reprobate has merits at life's end, he will be saved' is true, and this suffices for no falsehood to underlie hope.
claims: Infused hope expects beatitude only on the presupposition of merits.
Hope's truth is secured by a true conditional even in the reprobate.

HuYgTa-190886-Dd1e889.summary: Article 4, on the faith required before the Gospel, following Hugh of St Victor. Under the law of nature, belief in God as creator and expectation of salvation from him sufficed. Under the Mosaic law a mediator was announced without his nature being revealed, and under grace the mode of redemption and the person of the redeemer are openly preached. Explicit faith in each article was not required before the Gospel, though a minimum of explicit belief in God as creator and savior was always required and attainable by grace-enlightened reason in anyone doing what was in him. Objections from Augustine and from the analogy with charity are answered (one faith, differently explicit; natural instinct suffices for love but not for belief). The article closes with the reply to the opening argument about the hope of the reprobate.
claims: Before the Gospel, explicit faith in all the articles was not necessary for salvation.
A minimum of explicit faith, in God as creator and rewarding redeemer, was always necessary.
The faith of the ancients and moderns is one, differing in explicitness.
Infused hope is not false even in the reprobate, since it is conditioned on merits.
concepts: state of the law of nature

HuYgTa-190886.summary: Quaestio 1 on Distinctions 24-25: 'Whether falsehood can underlie faith'. Thomas answers in four articles. (1) Properly, the object of faith is God alone, the first truth to which all objects of belief are reduced; broadly, the articles and their annexes are its objects. (2) No falsehood can underlie infused faith, whether formed or unformed, because it comes from uncreated truth, posits contingent truths only as ordained by God, and rests on infallible divine authority; acquired faith, by contrast, can be false. Objections from prophecy, the timing of the Incarnation, Eucharistic adoration, God's absolute power and charity are answered with distinctions: nature vs divine power, opinion vs faith, conditional latria, absolute vs ordained power. (3) The articles are twelve, after the Apostles' Creed, and demonstrable truths are excluded. (4) Following Hugh of St Victor, before the Gospel only a minimum of explicit faith (God as creator and redeemer) was required, the faith of all ages being one but differently explicit. The opening argument from the false hope of the reprobate is answered by the conditional character of infused hope.
claims: God alone is the principal object of faith.
No falsehood can underlie infused faith; falsehood can underlie acquired faith.
Faith concerns contingent truths as ordained by God, i.e. under his ordained power.
There are twelve articles of faith; demonstrable truths are not articles.
Before the Gospel, only a minimum of explicit faith in God as creator and redeemer was necessary for salvation.
